topics.name: Martin Luther
topics.kicker: German monk turned reformer · Sparked the Protestant Reformation
topics.briefing: Martin Luther was a German monk who grew so troubled by the Catholic Church selling indulgences that he nailed ninety-five arguments against the practice to a church door in 1517. Ordered to take it all back, he refused, famously telling an emperor he was bound by Scripture and his own conscience. His stand split Western Christianity and started the Protestant Reformation, a movement whose name still describes hundreds of millions of Christians today.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) after excluding the Martin Luther King Jr. results that share the search

tossups.p: At the Marburg Colloquy, this man debated Huldrych Zwingli [“TSVING-lee”] over whether Christ was truly present in the bread and wine of the Eucharist. He had already condemned a bloody peasant uprising in a pamphlet called _Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants_, even though the rebels had drawn on his own ideas.
tossups.r: This man was threatened with excommunication by the papal bull _Exsurge Domine_. For 10 points, name this German monk who nailed the Ninety-Five Theses to a church door in Wittenberg and started the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: In a 1525 pamphlet titled _Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants_, this man urged German princes to crush a revolt that had drawn on his own religious ideas. Five years earlier, Pope Leo X had threatened this man with excommunication in the bull _Exsurge Domine_ [“ex-SUR-jay DOH-mih-nay”].
tossups.r: This man refused to recant his writings before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms in 1521. For 10 points, name this German reformer whose Ninety-Five Theses attacked the Catholic Church’s sale of indulgences.

tossups.p: Pope Leo X issued the bull _Exsurge Domine_ against this man in 1520, threatening him with excommunication unless he took back his writings within sixty days. This man refused, and formal excommunication followed the next year.
tossups.r: That same year, 1521, this man defended himself before the Diet of Worms [“vorms”], supposedly saying he could not act against his conscience. For 10 points, name this German monk who started the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: While hiding at Wartburg Castle under the disguise of a knight called Junker Jörg [“YOONG-ker YERG”], this man translated the New Testament into German so ordinary people could read it themselves. He later finished translating the whole Bible into German by 1534.
tossups.r: His translation used the recently invented printing press to spread quickly across the German states. For 10 points, name this reformer who had already nailed the Ninety-Five Theses to a church door in Wittenberg.

tossups.p: In 1521, this man stood before the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at an assembly in a German city and refused to take back what he had written, reportedly saying he was bound by Scripture and his own conscience.
tossups.r: That assembly was the Diet of Worms [“vorms”]. For 10 points, name this German monk whose Ninety-Five Theses had attacked the sale of indulgences and begun the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: Late in his life, this man drafted the Schmalkald [“SHMAHL-kahld”] Articles as a statement of belief for German princes who followed his teachings. Decades earlier, this man had taught theology at a university in the same small Saxon town where he would nail up his most famous work.
tossups.r: That town was Wittenberg. For 10 points, name this monk who posted the Ninety-Five Theses and launched the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man is said to have ended his defense at a 1521 imperial assembly with words to the effect of, “Here I stand; I can do no other.” He had already been excommunicated after refusing to recant ideas he first laid out in a document nailed to a church door four years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German reformer whose Ninety-Five Theses, posted in Wittenberg in 1517, began the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man was born in the Saxon mining town of Eisleben [“ICE-lay-ben”] in 1483 and later joined the Augustinian order of monks. As a young monk, he grew troubled by the Catholic Church’s sale of indulgences, documents said to reduce punishment for sin.
tossups.r: His objections to that practice became the Ninety-Five Theses. For 10 points, name this German monk who started the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man taught biblical theology at the University of Wittenberg [“VIT-en-berg”], where, according to tradition, he nailed a list of ninety-five complaints to the town church’s door on October 31, 1517. Some Protestant churches still celebrate that date as Reformation Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German monk whose Ninety-Five Theses protested the sale of indulgences and launched the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man designed a personal seal showing a black cross inside a red heart set on a white rose, a symbol still called by his name today. He explained the seal’s meaning in a 1530 letter, a year after he had debated Huldrych Zwingli at Marburg.
tossups.r: He had earlier hidden at Wartburg Castle, translating the New Testament into German. For 10 points, name this reformer who began the Protestant Reformation by posting the Ninety-Five Theses in Wittenberg.

tossups.p: Copies of this man’s most famous document spread across Germany within weeks, thanks to the recently invented printing press, even though he had only meant it for academic debate. Johann Tetzel [“TET-sel”], a friar who sold indulgences to help fund the rebuilding of St. Peter’s Basilica, was a chief target of that document.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German monk whose Ninety-Five Theses, posted in Wittenberg in 1517, began the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: In 1525, this man married a former nun named Katharina von Bora, and the couple eventually raised six children in a former monastery in Wittenberg. That same year, he urged German princes to crush a peasant revolt in a harshly worded pamphlet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German reformer who had earlier posted the Ninety-Five Theses and begun the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man wrote the words and music for the hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God,” which became an anthem of the religious movement he started. He based the hymn in part on the 46th Psalm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German monk whose Ninety-Five Theses, nailed to a church door in Wittenberg, began the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: Angered by the friar Johann Tetzel’s sales pitch that buying an indulgence could spring a relative’s soul from purgatory, this man wrote ninety-five arguments against the practice and, according to tradition, nailed them to a church door. Pope Leo X at first dismissed the dispute as a quarrel among monks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German theologian whose Ninety-Five Theses of 1517 began the Protestant Reformation.

tossups.p: This man died in 1546 in the same small German town where he had been born 62 years earlier, Eisleben, after preaching there on a trip to settle a dispute between two noble brothers. By then, his teachings had already split Western Christianity in two.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German reformer whose Ninety-Five Theses had begun the Protestant Reformation almost three decades earlier.

trap.title: Luther, not “Luther King”
trap.body: Quiz bowl sometimes confuses this German reformer with the American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who took this man’s last name as part of his own; King’s father renamed himself and his son after learning about the reformer on a trip to Germany. The two are not related. Luther is also easy to mix up with fellow reformers he argued with, like Huldrych Zwingli and John Calvin, who led their own branches of the Reformation.
trap.fix: The Ninety-Five Theses, the Diet of Worms, and the German Reformation mean Martin Luther. “I Have a Dream” and the civil rights movement mean Martin Luther King Jr. Zwingli (Zurich) and Calvin (Geneva) led their own, separate branches of the Reformation.

topics.name: World War I
topics.kicker: Global war, 1914–1918 · Trench warfare and a new, deadlier kind of combat
topics.briefing: World War I began in 1914 after a Bosnian assassin killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary, pulling Europe’s alliances into a war that most leaders expected to be over by Christmas. Instead, armies dug trenches across the Western Front and fought for years over a few miles of mud, while new weapons like machine guns, poison gas, and tanks made the fighting deadlier than ever. The war ended in 1918 with an armistice, and the Treaty of Versailles that followed reshaped the map of Europe.

sample.note: 9 real QBReader tossups (6 Middle School/Easy High School + 3 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: To knock France out quickly, German commanders followed the Schlieffen [“SHLEE-fen”] Plan and marched their armies through neutral Belgium, violating a treaty that Britain had promised to defend. That invasion of Belgium brought Britain into this war within days of its start in 1914.
tossups.r: Trench lines soon stretched across the Western Front from the English Channel to Switzerland. For 10 points, name this war fought mainly between the Allied and Central Powers from 1914 to 1918.

tossups.p: This conflict began after a Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip shot and killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary then declared war on Serbia, and a web of alliances pulled in Russia, Germany, France, and Britain within weeks.
tossups.r: Historians call that chain reaction the July Crisis. For 10 points, name this war, often called the Great War, that broke out in the summer of 1914.

tossups.p: Along much of its Western Front, this conflict became a stalemate of trench warfare, with soldiers on both sides living in muddy ditches separated by a deadly strip called No Man’s Land. New weapons used in this conflict included poison gas, machine guns, and, starting at the Somme in 1916, tanks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Britain, France, and their allies fought Germany and Austria-Hungary from 1914 to 1918.

tossups.p: Early in this war, French general Joseph Gallieni [“gal-YAY-nee”] famously rushed reinforcements to the front in requisitioned Paris taxicabs during the First Battle of the Marne, which stopped Germany’s advance and ended hopes of a quick victory. Four years of trench warfare followed on this war’s Western Front.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that also saw heavy fighting on an Eastern Front against Russia.

tossups.p: On this war’s Eastern Front, German commanders Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff [“LOO-den-dorf”] became national heroes after crushing a Russian army at the Battle of Tannenberg in 1914. Russia suffered further defeats before leaving this war after its 1917 revolution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that pitted the Central Powers against Russia, France, and Britain beginning in 1914.

tossups.p: A telegram from German official Arthur Zimmermann [“TSIM-er-mahn”], proposing a secret alliance with Mexico against the United States, was intercepted and published during this war, outraging American public opinion. Along with Germany’s resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare, that telegram helped push the United States to enter this war in 1917.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, in which General John Pershing then led the American Expeditionary Forces.

tossups.p: A German U-boat torpedoed the British liner _Lusitania_ in 1915 during this war, killing nearly 1,200 people, including well over a hundred Americans, and souring American opinion of Germany. Germany had declared the waters around Britain a war zone open to submarine attack.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, which the United States entered two years after that sinking.

tossups.p: British poet Wilfred Owen described a gas attack victim “guttering, choking, drowning” in a poem about this war titled “Dulce et Decorum Est” [“DUL-chay et deh-KOR-um EST”], which calls the Latin saying that it is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country “the old Lie.” Owen was killed in action just a week before this war ended.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, which also inspired Erich Maria Remarque’s novel _All Quiet on the Western Front_.

tossups.p: Fighting in this war stopped at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month of 1918, when an armistice took effect. Ordinary soldiers in this war were nicknamed “doughboys” in the American army and “Tommies” in the British one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that was, for a time, called “the war to end all wars.”

tossups.p: The treaty that ended this war forced Germany to accept blame in a “war guilt” clause, pay heavy reparations, and give up territory, while also creating the League of Nations. Woodrow Wilson had hoped for a gentler peace built on his Fourteen Points.
tossups.r: That treaty was signed at the palace of Versailles in 1919. For 10 points, name this war that had begun in 1914.

tossups.p: Winston Churchill lost his post as First Lord of the Admiralty during this war after planning a failed invasion of the Gallipoli [“guh-LIP-oh-lee”] Peninsula meant to open a supply route to Russia. Soldiers from Australia and New Zealand suffered heavy losses on Gallipoli’s beaches during this war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, whose Western Front saw far more Allied troops than Gallipoli ever did.

tossups.p: German pilot Manfred von Richthofen, nicknamed the “Red Baron,” shot down about eighty enemy aircraft during this war before he was killed in 1918. Earlier in this war, Britain lost about 20,000 men on a single day at the start of the Battle of the Somme.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that introduced tanks and fighter planes to modern combat.

tossups.p: Three royal cousins, Britain’s King George the Fifth, Germany’s Kaiser Wilhelm the Second, and Russia’s Tsar Nicholas the Second, ruled countries that ended up on opposite sides of this war, despite their close family ties. The tsar lost his throne and his life during this war.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that broke out among the royal cousins’ countries in 1914.

tossups.p: A mostly Black American regiment nicknamed the Harlem Hellfighters spent more days in front-line combat than almost any other American unit in this war. The American Expeditionary Forces, commanded by General John Pershing, arrived late in this war but helped turn the tide on the Western Front.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that the United States entered in 1917, more than two years after it began.

tossups.p: This war grew out of a tangle of causes that histories still summarize with the acronym MAIN: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism. Writers who came of age during this war, like Ernest Hemingway, became known as the “Lost Generation.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war that, despite hopes it would be “the war to end all wars,” was followed two decades later by an even larger global conflict.

trap.title: Which war? Which event?
trap.body: World War I shares territory with several related-but-different quiz bowl answers: the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand is the spark, not the war itself; the Treaty of Versailles is the document that ended it; and World War II, fought a generation later with many of the same countries, is a completely different war with its own battles and leaders. The Russian Civil War, which followed the 1917 Revolution, is also a separate conflict, even though it grew partly out of Russia leaving this one.
trap.fix: Trenches, the Western and Eastern Fronts, the Marne, Tannenberg, the Zimmermann Telegram, and 1914–1918 dates mean World War I. “Name this assassination” wants Franz Ferdinand’s murder; “name this treaty” wants Versailles. D-Day, the Holocaust, and Pearl Harbor all mean World War II instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: World War I (or WWI, the First World War)

topics.name: Charlemagne
topics.kicker: Frankish king crowned emperor in 800 · United much of Western Europe
topics.briefing: Charlemagne spent over four decades on horseback, conquering the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons in the north, and other peoples until he ruled most of Western Europe. On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome, the first time anyone had held that title in the West since Rome fell. At his court in Aachen, scholars like Einhard and Alcuin of York launched a revival of learning now called the Carolingian Renaissance.

sample.note: all 5 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This ruler besieged and captured Pavia [“PAH-vee-ah”] in 774, deposing the Lombard king Desiderius [“deh-sih-DAIR-ee-us”] and adding northern Italy to his realm. He had already begun a decades-long series of campaigns against the pagan Saxons in what is now northern Germany.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king who was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in the year 800.

tossups.p: The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid [“hah-ROON al-rah-SHEED”] once sent this ruler an elephant named Abul-Abbas and an elaborate water clock as diplomatic gifts. This ruler’s rear guard, which included the commander Roland, was ambushed by Basque fighters at Roncevaux Pass [“ron-suh-VOH”] in 778, an event later mythologized in the _Song of Roland_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king who united much of Western Europe and was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.

tossups.p: This ruler’s rear guard was wiped out by Basque raiders at Roncevaux Pass in 778 while returning from a campaign in Spain, a defeat that medieval poets later reimagined as a last stand against Muslim armies in the _Song of Roland_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king, crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800, whose nephew Roland supposedly died at Roncevaux.

tossups.p: This ruler’s friend and court scholar Einhard wrote an admiring biography of him, modeled on the style of ancient Roman biographies. Scholars such as Einhard and Alcuin of York gathered at this ruler’s palace school in Aachen, sparking a revival of learning and Latin scholarship.
tossups.r: Historians call that revival a “Renaissance” named for this ruler’s dynasty. For 10 points, name this Frankish king, inspiration for the Carolingian Renaissance.

tossups.p: This ruler invited the English scholar Alcuin of York [“AL-kwin”] to run the palace school at his capital, Aachen [“AH-ken”], helping spark a revival of Latin learning and manuscript copying. This ruler could reportedly read but never learned to write well himself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king and Carolingian Renaissance patron who was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

tossups.p: This ruler’s grandfather, Charles Martel [“mar-TEL”], had turned back a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours but never claimed a royal title for himself. This ruler, by contrast, accepted the title of emperor from the pope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grandson of Charles Martel who united the Franks and was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

tossups.p: This ruler’s father, Pepin the Short, had become the first Carolingian king of the Franks by deposing the last of the “do-nothing” Merovingian kings with the pope’s blessing. This ruler inherited that throne and then expanded it dramatically.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this son of Pepin the Short who conquered the Lombards and Saxons and was crowned emperor in Rome.

tossups.p: This ruler briefly shared the Frankish throne with his younger brother Carloman after their father’s death, until Carloman died just three years later and left this ruler sole king. Some accounts suggest the brothers were on the edge of civil war when that death occurred.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king who then ruled alone for over 40 years and was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

tossups.p: This ruler spent more than thirty years fighting the pagan Saxons in brutal campaigns across northern Germany, at one point reportedly ordering the execution of thousands of Saxon prisoners at Verden. He eventually forced the Saxons to convert to Christianity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king who also conquered the Lombards in Italy and was crowned emperor by the pope in 800.

tossups.p: Beyond Italy and Saxony, this ruler’s armies also conquered Bavaria and pushed Frankish control south of the Pyrenees into a buffer zone of northern Spain called the Spanish March. His empire eventually stretched across most of Western Europe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king who was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in 800.

tossups.p: After this ruler’s death, his empire passed whole to his one surviving legitimate son, Louis the Pious, but Louis’s own three sons later split it into three kingdoms at the Treaty of Verdun in 843. Two of those kingdoms roughly became the later France and Germany.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this grandfather of the quarreling princes, a Frankish king crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

tossups.p: According to his biographer Einhard, this ruler was genuinely surprised when Pope Leo III placed a crown on his head while he knelt in prayer at Old St. Peter’s Basilica, though many historians doubt the coronation was really a surprise.
tossups.r: That coronation happened on Christmas Day in the year 800. For 10 points, name this Frankish king who became the first emperor crowned in the West in centuries.

tossups.p: This ruler built a favorite palace at Aachen, a city known for its hot springs, where he was later buried in the cathedral he had built there. He also ordered the construction of a canal, the Fossa Carolina, meant to link the Rhine and Danube river systems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king and emperor whose palace chapel at Aachen still stands today.

tossups.p: This ruler introduced a new silver-based currency system across his realm, along with standard weights and measures, to make trade easier between his many conquered territories. He also pushed bishops and monasteries to open schools for ordinary clergy, not just nobles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king and economic reformer who was crowned Emperor of the Romans in 800.

tossups.p: This ruler is sometimes nicknamed the “Father of Europe” for uniting so much of the continent under Frankish rule, even though he himself reportedly never mastered writing. Later rulers of both France and the Holy Roman Empire traced their legitimacy back to him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Frankish king, crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III in the year 800.

trap.title: Charlemagne, not his family
trap.body: Charlemagne’s own family tree is full of quiz bowl traps: his grandfather Charles Martel won the Battle of Tours but was never king; his father Pepin the Short founded the Carolingian dynasty; and his son Louis the Pious inherited the whole empire, which Louis’s own sons later split up at the Treaty of Verdun. Real answer lines accept “Charles I” for Charlemagne but specifically warn against accepting “Charles Martel” instead. Historians also usually date the formal “Holy Roman Empire” from Otto the Great’s coronation in 962, more than a century after Charlemagne’s own crowning as emperor in 800.
trap.fix: Pavia, the Lombards, Aachen, Einhard, Alcuin, and a coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800 mean Charlemagne. Tours and “the Hammer” mean Charles Martel; the Treaty of Verdun and squabbling grandsons mean Louis the Pious’s sons; Otto the Great starts the usual timeline for the Holy Roman Empire.

Harold had just force-marched south after beating a Viking invasion at Stamford Bridge, and he was killed in the fighting — legend says by an arrow to the eye, as shown on the embroidered _Bayeux Tapestry_. tossups.p: Pope Alexander II blessed the invading side’s banner before this battle, in which archers and mounted knights backed the attackers while their opponents fought entirely on foot. Two of the losing king’s brothers, Gyrth and Leofwine, died defending him here, fighting alongside men armed with long battle-axes.
tossups.r: Norman horsemen staged fake retreats to pull defenders off a ridge and break apart their wall of shields. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William the Conqueror defeated Harold Godwinson.

tossups.p: Weeks before this battle, the losing side’s troops had just defeated a Norwegian invasion, killing both King Harald Hardrada [“HAR-uld HARD-rah-duh”] and the English king’s own exiled brother Tostig. Those exhausted troops then marched roughly two hundred miles south in a matter of days to meet a second invading army near England’s coast.
tossups.r: The invaders’ cavalry staged fake retreats to break apart a shield wall atop a ridge. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William the Conqueror defeated King Harold II of England.

tossups.p: The winning commander in this battle claimed that the childless King Edward the Confessor had already promised him the English crown, and that his rival had once sworn, while shipwrecked in Normandy years earlier, to support that claim. England’s nobles, the Witenagemot [“WIT-en-uh-geh-mot”], had instead chosen that rival as king.
tossups.r: That rival was Harold Godwinson. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle, William the Conqueror’s decisive victory over Harold in England.

tossups.p: A Norman ally named Eustace of Boulogne was wounded during this battle, in which retreating soldiers made a desperate last stand in a ditch later called the Malfosse [“mal-FOSS”]. Most of the fighting took place on a ridge known to some chroniclers as Senlac Hill.
tossups.r: William the Conqueror won this battle over King Harold II. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle that began the Norman Conquest of England.

tossups.p: Odo, the Bishop of Bayeux [“bai-YOO”] and half-brother of this battle’s winning commander, is thought to have commissioned a famous 230-foot embroidery depicting it. That commander later built an abbey on the site, with tradition holding that its altar marked the exact spot where his rival fell.
tossups.r: His rival was Harold Godwinson, killed in the fighting. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle won by William the Conqueror.

tossups.p: This battle lasted most of a single day, beginning around nine in the morning and dragging on until dusk. Weeks earlier, the eventual winner had sailed an invasion fleet across the English Channel from Normandy, landing on England’s southern coast in late September.
tossups.r: William the Conqueror’s fleet finally met Harold Godwinson’s army in this battle. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle that began Norman rule of England.

tossups.p: One side in this battle formed a shield wall using housecarls, the king’s elite bodyguards, along with fyrd levies of ordinary freemen. That side had no cavalry and very few archers of its own, unlike its opponents.
tossups.r: The shield wall held for hours atop a ridge before finally breaking. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William the Conqueror defeated the English king.

tossups.p: Twenty years after this battle, its winner ordered a massive survey of English land and property later called the _Domesday Book_. That same winner brought Norman French words and nobles into England, reshaping its language and ruling class for centuries.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1066 battle, William the Conqueror’s victory over Harold Godwinson that began the Norman Conquest of England.

tossups.p: Chroniclers say the losing king in this battle was struck by an arrow near the eye, a death shown in one famous scene of the _Bayeux Tapestry_. That same embroidered artwork depicts the whole Norman invasion leading up to this fight.
tossups.r: Harold Godwinson died in this battle. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William the Conqueror conquered England.

tossups.p: Its winning commander became known ever after by an epithet referring to this battle’s outcome, and was crowned King of England in London before the year was out. His rival had been chosen by the Witenagemot just months earlier.
tossups.r: That winning commander was William the Conqueror. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which he defeated Harold Godwinson, ending Anglo-Saxon rule of England.

tossups.p: Among the dead in this battle were Gyrth and Leofwine, both brothers of the English king, who fell defending him atop Senlac Hill. Norman cavalry had to charge the ridge repeatedly before the defenders’ line finally gave way.
tossups.r: The English king himself, Harold Godwinson, was killed soon after. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle, William the Conqueror’s victory in southern England.

tossups.p: English nobles called the Witenagemot [“WIT-en-uh-geh-mot”] had elected the loser of this battle king only months before, passing over a Norman duke who insisted the dead King Edward the Confessor had already promised him the throne.
tossups.r: That Norman duke, William, won this battle instead. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle that gave William the Conqueror the English crown.

tossups.p: A wounded Norman ally, Eustace of Boulogne, survived this battle, in which some of the defeated army made a final stand in a ditch nicknamed the Malfosse after the main fighting ended. The battle was fought on a ridge soon after an exhausting forced march from the north.
tossups.r: That march followed a victory at Stamford Bridge. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William the Conqueror defeated the English army.

tossups.p: William the Conqueror later built Battle Abbey on the site of this fight, with legend placing its high altar at the exact spot where his rival died. Years afterward, William ordered the detailed land survey known as the _Domesday Book_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1066 battle in which William defeated and killed Harold Godwinson, beginning the Norman Conquest of England.

tossups.p: Before this battle, the English army had just force-marched south after a brutal win over Vikings at Stamford Bridge, where King Harald Hardrada and the English king’s brother Tostig were both killed. That exhausted army then formed a shield wall to face a second, fresh invading force.
tossups.r: William the Conqueror’s Normans broke that shield wall. For 10 points, name this 1066 battle that ended Anglo-Saxon rule of England.

trap.title: Stamford Bridge vs. Hastings
trap.body: Harold Godwinson fought — and won — the Battle of Stamford Bridge against a Viking army just weeks before marching south to lose this battle, so clues about defeating Harald Hardrada or Tostig describe that earlier, different battle. Questions also lean on the famous “arrow to the eye” story from the _Bayeux Tapestry_, even though historians aren’t fully certain that is exactly how Harold died.
trap.fix: A Viking invasion in the north that Harold wins is Stamford Bridge. William landing in the south and Harold losing — and dying — is this battle. Say “Hastings,” not just “Norman Conquest,” which is the whole era this battle began.

topics.name: Crusades
topics.kicker: Christian wars to retake the Holy Land · 1096–1291
topics.briefing: Starting in 1096, European Christians launched a series of military campaigns called the Crusades to capture and defend the Holy Land from Muslim rule. Pope Urban II kicked off the First Crusade by calling Christians to “take back” Jerusalem, which crusaders captured in 1099. Later Crusades featured larger-than-life rivals like Richard the Lionheart and Saladin, and even veered off target — the Fourth Crusade sacked the Christian city of Constantinople instead.

sample.note: the 5 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One of these conflicts, led by Simon de Montfort against the Cathars of southern France, included the Battle of Muret and the Siege of Carcassonne [“kar-kuh-SON”] rather than any fighting in the Middle East. Another of these campaigns began after Guy de Lusignan’s army was crushed at the Horns of Hattin [“hah-TEEN”] in 1187, a defeat that let Saladin retake Jerusalem.
tossups.r: England’s Richard the Lionheart later fought Saladin to a truce in the third of these wars. For 10 points, name this series of medieval military campaigns in which European Christians tried to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: An anonymous chronicle called the _Gesta Francorum_ [“JESS-tuh fran-KOR-um”] recorded the first of these campaigns, which was partly led by a preacher named Peter the Hermit. Crusader nobles passing through Byzantine territory at the start of this campaign often had to swear loyalty oaths to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos.
tossups.r: That first campaign ended with a victory at the Battle of Ascalon in 1099, after capturing Jerusalem. For 10 points, name this series of wars fought by medieval Christians to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: During one of these conflicts, the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned while crossing the Saleph River in modern Turkey. That same campaign saw Richard the Lionheart defeat Saladin’s forces at the Battle of Arsuf in 1191, though Jerusalem itself stayed in Muslim hands.
tossups.r: Richard and Saladin eventually agreed to a truce allowing Christian pilgrims to visit the city. For 10 points, name this series of medieval military campaigns to capture the Holy Land.

tossups.p: One of these campaigns never reached the Middle East at all: crusaders diverted by Venetian merchants instead sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204. A much earlier campaign in this series, called after Muslim forces captured the crusader county of Edessa, ended in failure.
tossups.r: The first of these campaigns, by contrast, succeeded in capturing Jerusalem in 1099. For 10 points, name this series of wars fought between European Christians and Muslims over the Holy Land.

tossups.p: France’s King Louis IX was captured in Egypt soon after the Battle of Al Mansurah [“al man-SOO-rah”] during one of these campaigns, and had to be ransomed. That same king later died of disease in Tunisia while leading another of these wars decades afterward.
tossups.r: Louis IX never gave up trying to retake the Holy Land. For 10 points, name this series of medieval conflicts fought by Christian Europe against Muslim powers.

tossups.p: Pope Urban II launched the first of these campaigns at the Council of Clermont in 1095, and crowds reportedly shouted “Deus vult,” meaning “God wills it,” in support. Godfrey of Bouillon [“boo-YOHN”] became the new crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem’s first ruler after that campaign succeeded.
tossups.r: Godfrey’s brother Baldwin later became the first to actually use the title “King of Jerusalem.” For 10 points, name this series of wars to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: Military religious orders such as the Knights Templar and Knights Hospitaller formed to protect pilgrims and fight during these campaigns. Italian city-states like Venice and Genoa grew wealthy transporting soldiers and supplies for this series of wars.
tossups.r: The first of these campaigns captured Jerusalem for European Christians in 1099. For 10 points, name this series of medieval military expeditions to the Holy Land.

tossups.p: Saladin’s crushing victory over Guy de Lusignan’s army at the Horns of Hattin in 1187 let Muslim forces retake Jerusalem, provoking a furious response from European kings. That response became the third of these campaigns, which starred Richard the Lionheart.
tossups.r: Earlier, the first of these campaigns had captured the same city in 1099. For 10 points, name this series of wars between Christian Europe and Muslim powers over the Holy Land.

tossups.p: Not every campaign in this series targeted Muslims: one, led by Simon de Montfort, instead attacked Christian heretics called the Cathars in southern France. Much later, England’s Prince Edward, the future King Edward I, led the last major campaign in this series to the Holy Land.
tossups.r: That final campaign accomplished little before Edward returned home to become king. For 10 points, name this series of medieval wars, most of which targeted the Holy Land.

tossups.p: The second of these campaigns, called after Muslim forces seized the crusader county of Edessa, ended in failure. Decades earlier, the first of these campaigns, recorded in an anonymous chronicle called the _Gesta Francorum_, had succeeded where the second failed.
tossups.r: Pope Urban II had launched the first of these wars at the Council of Clermont. For 10 points, name this series of conflicts fought to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: English and French kings joined forces with the Holy Roman Emperor to launch the third of these campaigns after Saladin recaptured Jerusalem. Only one of those monarchs, Richard the Lionheart, stayed to fight after Frederick Barbarossa drowned and the French king went home early.
tossups.r: Richard won the Battle of Arsuf but ultimately settled for a truce with Saladin. For 10 points, name this series of wars to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: Venetian merchants helped redirect one of these campaigns toward a fellow Christian city rather than toward Muslim-held territory, after crusaders ran up debts they could not pay. That campaign’s army sacked Constantinople in 1204 and set up a short-lived Latin Empire there instead.
tossups.r: That badly misdirected campaign never reached the Holy Land at all. For 10 points, name this series of medieval military expeditions, most of which targeted Jerusalem.

tossups.p: A wave of common people with little military training marched toward the Holy Land at the start of this series of wars, inspired by the preaching of Peter the Hermit. Most of them never reached their goal, but trained knights following behind captured Jerusalem in 1099.
tossups.r: Godfrey of Bouillon then ruled the new crusader kingdom there. For 10 points, name this series of conflicts in which European Christians fought to control the Holy Land.

tossups.p: France’s King Louis IX led two separate campaigns in this series: in one, he was captured in Egypt after the Battle of Al Mansurah and had to be ransomed; in a later one, he died of disease in Tunisia. Those were the seventh and eighth of these wars.
tossups.r: Despite Louis’s efforts, Christian power in the Holy Land kept shrinking. For 10 points, name this series of medieval wars fought over Jerusalem and the surrounding region.

tossups.p: Jerusalem changed hands more than once during this series of conflicts: European knights captured it in 1099, lost it to Saladin in 1187, and never permanently held it again despite several later campaigns. Richard the Lionheart marched close to it but turned back during the third of these wars.
tossups.r: Pope Urban II had launched the first of these campaigns to retake the city from Muslim rule. For 10 points, name this series of medieval military expeditions to the Holy Land.

trap.title: Which Henry?
trap.body: England had eight kings named Henry, and quiz bowl asks about several of them. His father, Henry VII, won the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 and started the Tudor dynasty, and Henry V won the Battle of Agincourt in the Hundred Years’ War. Saying just “Henry” earns a prompt, and the wrong number is simply wrong. One real tossup even wanted only the name “Henry,” with a clue about Henry IV of France and the Edict of Nantes mixed in.
trap.fix: Six wives, the split from Rome, the Act of Supremacy, Thomas Cromwell, or Thomas More mean Henry VIII. Bosworth Field and the first Tudor mean Henry VII; Agincourt and the “band of brothers” speech mean Henry V. Always say the number: “Henry the Eighth.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Henry VIII (or Henry the 8th; prompt on Henry)

sample.note: 11 real QBReader tossups (5 Middle School/Easy High School + 6 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This war’s first major battle was fought at sea off Sluys, where an English fleet destroyed a French one in 1340. This war had begun three years earlier, after Philip VI of France seized English lands in Gascony and Edward III of England claimed the French crown.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this long war between England and France that lasted from 1337 to 1453.

tossups.p: At one battle in this war, the blind King John of Bohemia had his knights tie their horses to his so that he could ride into the fight, where he was killed. At that 1346 battle, Crécy [“kray-SEE”], English archers cut down charge after charge of French knights.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which England and France fought from 1337 to 1453.

tossups.p: A French peasant revolt called the Jacquerie [“zhah-kuh-REE”] broke out in 1358, two years after the king of France was captured in this war. That king, John II, had lost the Battle of Poitiers [“pwah-TYAY”] to Edward the Black Prince, who had fought at Crécy as a teenager.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war between England and France that later featured Joan of Arc.

tossups.p: The Treaty of Troyes [“TWAH”] in this war named England’s king as heir to the French throne and arranged his marriage to Catherine of Valois. That English king had won a famous victory at Agincourt [“AJ-in-kort”] five years earlier.
tossups.r: That king was Henry V. For 10 points, name this war between England and France that lasted more than a century.

tossups.p: This war’s last major battle was fought at Castillon [“kass-tee-YOHN”] in 1453, where French cannons shattered an English army and its commander, John Talbot, was killed. That defeat left England holding only the port of Calais [“ka-LAY”] in France.
tossups.r: Joan of Arc had fought in this war decades earlier. For 10 points, name this war that, despite its name, lasted 116 years.

tossups.p: Auguste Rodin’s sculpture _The Burghers of Calais_ shows six town leaders who offered their lives to England’s Edward III after a long siege in this war. Queen Philippa persuaded her husband to spare them, and England then held Calais [“ka-LAY”] until 1558.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war between England and France, fought from 1337 to 1453.

tossups.p: In one battle of this war, French knights in heavy armor struggled across a muddy, freshly plowed field while English archers sheltered behind sharpened wooden stakes. The Constable of France, Charles d’Albret [“dahl-BRAY”], was among the many French nobles killed that day.
tossups.r: That battle was Agincourt. For 10 points, name this war in which Henry V defeated the French.

tossups.p: The Treaty of Brétigny [“bray-teen-YEE”] paused this war in 1360, giving England a large part of southwestern France in exchange for Edward III agreeing to give up his claim to the French crown. That treaty also set a huge ransom for a French king captured four years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Joan of Arc later fought for France against England.

tossups.p: Jean Froissart [“frwah-SAR”] wrote chronicles of this war, describing knights, sieges, and battles such as Crécy and Poitiers. In this war’s later years, France was torn between two rival groups, the Armagnacs and the Burgundians, until the Treaty of Arras brought Burgundy back to the French side in 1435.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war, fought from 1337 to 1453, in which Joan of Arc served France.

tossups.p: Poll taxes raised to pay for this war helped spark England’s Peasants’ Revolt of 1381. Decades earlier in this war, the Black Death swept through both England and France and slowed the fighting for several years.
tossups.r: Later, English archers won at Agincourt. For 10 points, name this war in which Joan of Arc helped France defeat England.

tossups.p: In a Shakespeare history play, a king rallies his outnumbered troops during this war with a speech about “we few, we happy few, we band of brothers.” He gives that speech before a battle on St. Crispin’s Day in 1415.
tossups.r: That battle was Agincourt. For 10 points, name this long war between England and France.

tossups.p: In 1431, an English-controlled church court in Rouen [“roo-AHN”] convicted a young prisoner of heresy during this war, and she was burned at the stake. Two years earlier, that young woman had led French troops to break the Siege of Orléans [“or-lay-AHN”].
tossups.r: That woman was Joan of Arc. For 10 points, name this war between England and France.

tossups.p: The French heir Charles VII was crowned at Reims in 1429 during this war, even though his own father had once signed a treaty naming an English king as heir to France. A teenage girl who had just won a key siege stood near Charles at the ceremony.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Joan of Arc led French troops against England.

tossups.p: English armies in this war often used the chevauchée [“sheh-voh-SHAY”], a mounted raid that burned crops and villages across the French countryside. Edward the Black Prince led one such raid shortly before winning the Battle of Poitiers in 1356.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which English longbowmen won at Crécy and Agincourt.

tossups.p: When he was just ten years old, England’s Henry VI was crowned King of France in Paris during this war, while his uncle, the Duke of Bedford, governed English-held France for him. Henry VI’s father had won the Battle of Agincourt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this war in which Joan of Arc fought to drive the English out of France.

clues.t: Fought between England and France, as English kings claimed the French crown
Lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, despite its name
Joan of Arc, a teenage peasant girl, led the French to break the Siege of Orléans (1429)
Henry V won the Battle of Agincourt (1415), fought on St. Crispin’s Day
English longbowmen beat French knights again and again
Battle of Crécy (1346): Edward III’s archers beat a larger French army
Battle of Poitiers (1356): Edward the Black Prince defeated King John II of France, who was taken prisoner

Joan of Arc brought the French heir Charles VII to be crowned at Reims (1429)
Joan was captured, convicted of heresy by an English-backed church court, and burned at the stake in Rouen (1431)
Shakespeare’s _Henry V_ has the “band of brothers” speech before Agincourt
When it ended, England held only the port of Calais, which it kept until 1558
Battle of Castillon (1453), the last battle: French cannons won, and English commander John Talbot was killed
At Agincourt, French knights struggled through mud while English archers sheltered behind sharpened stakes
The blind King John of Bohemia rode into battle at Crécy tied to his knights and was killed
Battle of Sluys (1340): an English naval victory, its first major battle
Treaty of Brétigny (1360) paused the fighting and set King John II’s ransom
Treaty of Troyes (1420): Henry V married Catherine of Valois and was named heir to the French throne
Charles d’Albret, the Constable of France, was killed at Agincourt
The Jacquerie (1358): a French peasant revolt after King John II was captured
The Burgundians sided with England until the Treaty of Arras (1435)
Jean Froissart wrote its most famous chronicles
Rodin’s _The Burghers of Calais_ honors six leaders who offered their lives to Edward III (1347)
Poll taxes to pay for it helped spark England’s Peasants’ Revolt (1381)
English armies used the chevauchée, a raid that burned crops and villages across the French countryside
Henry VI was crowned King of France in Paris (1431) while his uncle, the Duke of Bedford, ruled for him

trap.title: Count the years
trap.body: Quiz bowl has a whole family of “number” wars. The Hundred Years’ War was England vs. France (1337–1453); the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) was fought mostly in the Holy Roman Empire; the Seven Years’ War (1756–1763) included the French and Indian War; and the Eighty Years’ War was the Dutch revolt against Spain. Napoleon’s “Hundred Days” (1815) sounds close but is a different answer, and a QBReader search for “Hundred Years” also turns up the novel _One Hundred Years of Solitude_.
trap.fix: Medieval clues (knights, longbows, Joan of Arc, Agincourt, Crécy, Poitiers, the Black Prince) mean the Hundred Years’ War. Catholics vs. Protestants and the Defenestration of Prague mean the Thirty Years’ War. Say the whole name: just “Hundred Years” only earns a prompt.

media.note: Quick read: Corsica to emperor, Russia, Waterloo, plus fun facts (was he really short?)

qb.tip: Napoleon is #1 on QBReader’s European History frequency list (10 Middle School and Easy High School tossups), the most-asked answer in the whole category. Skip the one result whose answer is the Napoleonic Wars, and notice that one answer line says not to accept Napoleon III.

sample.note: the 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A young German named Friedrich Staps was arrested at a military parade in Vienna in 1809 for trying to assassinate this ruler, who questioned him in person. Later that year, this ruler ended his marriage to Josephine because she had not given him an heir.
tossups.r: He then married Marie Louise of Austria. For 10 points, name this French emperor who was defeated at Waterloo.

tossups.p: A bomb called the “infernal machine” exploded on a Paris street in 1800, just after this leader’s carriage passed by. At the time, this leader ruled France as First Consul, a post he had seized in the Coup of 18 Brumaire [“broo-MAIR”].
tossups.r: Four years later, he crowned himself emperor. For 10 points, name this Corsican-born ruler of France.

tossups.p: As a young artillery officer, this man first won fame by helping drive the British out of the port of Toulon [“too-LOHN”] in 1793. Two years later, he used cannon fire to break up a royalist uprising in the streets of Paris.
tossups.r: He later lost the Battle of Waterloo. For 10 points, name this general who became Emperor of the French.

tossups.p: This general named one of his war horses Marengo after his 1800 victory over the Austrians in northern Italy. Jacques-Louis David painted this general crossing the Alps at the Great St. Bernard Pass on a rearing horse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French emperor who was finally exiled to Saint Helena.

tossups.p: This ruler forced Austria to give up land in the Treaty of Pressburg after his victory at Austerlitz, the “Battle of the Three Emperors,” in 1805. Only weeks before that victory, Horatio Nelson had crushed a French and Spanish fleet at Trafalgar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French emperor who was defeated at Waterloo in 1815.

tossups.p: This ruler called his 1812 invasion of Russia the “Second Polish War.” After winning a costly battle against Mikhail Kutuzov [“koo-TOO-zuff”] at Borodino [“bor-uh-DEE-noh”], his Grande Armée [“grahnd ar-MAY”] reached Moscow, only to find the city in flames.
tossups.r: Most of his army was lost during the retreat through the Russian winter. For 10 points, name this French emperor who was later defeated at Waterloo.

tossups.p: During this general’s invasion of Egypt, French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, and scholars he brought along began studying ancient Egyptian ruins. Horatio Nelson destroyed this general’s fleet at the Battle of the Nile, leaving his army stranded.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French leader who later crowned himself emperor and lost at Waterloo.

tossups.p: This ruler’s Berlin and Milan Decrees set up the Continental System, which tried to ruin Britain’s economy by banning European trade with it. Portugal’s refusal to join that blockade led this ruler to invade the Iberian Peninsula.
tossups.r: That invasion started the Peninsular War. For 10 points, name this French emperor who lost at Waterloo.

tossups.p: Ludwig van Beethoven angrily scratched this ruler’s name off the title page of his Third Symphony, the _Eroica_, after this man declared himself emperor. This man’s coronation in 1804, with Pope Pius VII looking on, was painted by Jacques-Louis David.
tossups.r: He was later exiled to Elba and to Saint Helena. For 10 points, name this Corsican-born Emperor of the French.

tossups.p: This emperor met Tsar Alexander I on a raft in the middle of the Neman River before they signed the Treaties of Tilsit in 1807. A year earlier, he had grouped many German states into the Confederation of the Rhine.
tossups.r: That move helped end the Holy Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this French emperor who lost at Waterloo.

tossups.p: After his army failed to retake the rebellious colony of Saint-Domingue [“san doh-MANG”], this leader sold the huge Louisiana Territory to the United States in 1803 for about 15 million dollars. That colony soon became the independent nation of Haiti.
tossups.r: He also introduced a single civil code of laws for all of France. For 10 points, name this French leader who crowned himself emperor in 1804.

tossups.p: In 1815, this man escaped from Elba, landed in southern France, and won over the soldiers sent to arrest him, starting the Hundred Days. The Seventh Coalition, led by the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian general Blücher [“BLOO-kur”], ended that comeback.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French emperor who spent his last years in exile on Saint Helena.

tossups.p: This ruler made his older brother Joseph the unpopular king of Spain in 1808, during the Peninsular War. In 1813, this ruler lost the Battle of Leipzig [“LIPE-sig”], also called the Battle of the Nations, and the next year he was exiled to Elba.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French emperor whose final defeat came at Waterloo in 1815.

tossups.p: This leader reached the Concordat of 1801 with Pope Pius VII, making peace between the French government and the Catholic Church after the Revolution. This leader’s first wife, Josephine, was crowned empress at Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1804.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French emperor who was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to Saint Helena.

tossups.p: This man’s remains were brought back to Paris in 1840 and now lie in a huge tomb under the dome of Les Invalides [“lay zan-vah-LEED”]. In 1806, he ordered the building of the Arc de Triomphe to honor the soldiers of his Grande Armée.
tossups.r: Admirers called him “the Little Corporal.” For 10 points, name this Corsican-born emperor of France.

clues.t: Lost the Battle of Waterloo (1815) to the Duke of Wellington and the Prussians
Crowned himself Emperor of the French at Notre-Dame in 1804
Died in exile on Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic (1821)
Born on the Mediterranean island of Corsica (1769)
Battle of Austerlitz (1805): beat Austria and Russia in the “Battle of the Three Emperors,” his greatest victory
Invaded Russia in 1812; reached a burning Moscow, then lost most of his army retreating in winter
Lost at Leipzig (1813), was exiled to Elba (1814), then escaped for the Hundred Days (1815)
Fought seven coalitions of European powers; the Seventh Coalition finally beat him
Horatio Nelson destroyed a French and Spanish fleet at Trafalgar (1805), ending his hopes of invading Britain
First wife Josephine; he divorced her for lack of an heir and married Marie Louise of Austria (1810)
His Civil Code (1804) gave all of France one set of laws, and it still bears his name
Sold the Louisiana Territory to the United States (1803) after failing to retake Saint-Domingue (Haiti)
Nicknamed “the Little Corporal”; the idea that he was very short is mostly a myth
Made his brother Joseph king of Spain (1808) and fought the British, Spanish, and Portuguese in the Peninsular War
Invaded Egypt (1798): his soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, but Nelson sank his fleet at the Battle of the Nile
Continental System (Berlin and Milan Decrees): tried to ruin Britain by banning European trade with it
Won the costly Battle of Borodino (1812) against Kutuzov’s Russian army
Treaty of Pressburg (1805) took land from Austria after Austerlitz
Seized power in the Coup of 18 Brumaire (1799) and ruled as First Consul
First won fame as an artillery officer at the Siege of Toulon (1793)
Named one of his horses Marengo after his 1800 victory over Austria
Friedrich Staps tried to assassinate him at a parade in Vienna (1809)
Survived the “infernal machine,” a bomb set off near his carriage in Paris (1800)
Called his invasion of Russia the “Second Polish War”
Treaties of Tilsit (1807): met Tsar Alexander I on a raft in the Neman River
Beethoven scratched his name off the dedication of the _Eroica_ Symphony when he became emperor
Jacques-Louis David painted his coronation and showed him crossing the Alps on a rearing horse

trap.title: Which Napoleon? Which answer?
trap.body: Napoleon I (Napoleon Bonaparte) is the famous emperor; his nephew Louis-Napoleon became Napoleon III, Emperor of the French from 1852 until he was captured at Sedan in the Franco-Prussian War. Real answer lines say “do NOT accept or prompt on Napoleon III,” and saying only “Bonaparte” gets a prompt. Napoleon and Waterloo tossups share clues like Wellington, Blücher, and Saint Helena, so the last line decides the answer.
trap.fix: “Name this emperor” (or this general, or this leader) wants Napoleon; “name this battle” wants Waterloo; “name this conflict” wants the Napoleonic Wars. Sedan, the Crimean War, and Baron Haussmann’s rebuilding of Paris mean Napoleon III. Say “Napoleon,” not just “Bonaparte.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Napoleon Bonaparte (or Napoleon I; prompt on Bonaparte; do NOT accept or prompt on “Napoleon III”)

topics.name: Otto von Bismarck
topics.briefing: Otto von Bismarck said the big questions of his time would be settled not by speeches but by “iron and blood,” and he meant it. As Prussia’s leader, he won three short wars in seven years, against Denmark, Austria, and France, and in 1871 he united the German states into one German Empire. As its first chancellor, he also created the world’s first national health insurance and old-age pensions.

sample.note: 16 real QBReader tossups (4 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: While this man was Prussia’s ambassador in Paris in 1862, War Minister Albrecht von Roon sent him a telegram urging him to hurry home because there was “danger in delay.” Days after returning, he became Prussia’s Minister President and fought the legislature over a bigger army budget.
tossups.r: Soon after, he gave his famous “blood and iron” speech. For 10 points, name this Prussian “Iron Chancellor.”

tossups.p: This statesman’s Gastein Convention of 1865 split control of two duchies between Prussia and Austria, an arrangement that soon broke down. That breakdown led to a war that Prussia won in just seven weeks after a decisive victory at Königgrätz [“KUR-nig-grets”].
tossups.r: Those duchies were Schleswig and Holstein. For 10 points, name this Prussian leader who later united Germany as its “Iron Chancellor.”

tossups.p: This leader’s education minister, Adalbert Falk, pushed through the May Laws, which put the training of Catholic priests under state control. Those laws were part of this leader’s Kulturkampf [“kool-TOOR-kahmpf”], or “culture struggle,” against the Catholic Church.
tossups.r: This leader also provoked a war with France by editing the Ems Dispatch. For 10 points, name this first chancellor of the German Empire.

tossups.p: Leo von Caprivi [“kah-PREE-vee”] replaced this man in 1890, the year that a John Tenniel cartoon in _Punch_ magazine showed this man walking down a ship’s ladder as the young emperor watched from the deck. That cartoon was titled “Dropping the Pilot.”
tossups.r: Kaiser Wilhelm II had forced him out. For 10 points, name this “Iron Chancellor” who had unified Germany.

tossups.p: This diplomat created the Three Emperors’ League with Austria-Hungary and Russia, and after it collapsed, he arranged a secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887. Once he left office, Germany let that treaty lapse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this German chancellor who had said that great questions would be decided by “blood and iron.”

tossups.p: This statesman promised to act as an “honest broker” at the 1878 Congress of Berlin, which he hosted to rewrite the Treaty of San Stefano after a war between Russia and the Ottoman Empire. A year later, he formed the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary.
tossups.r: Italy joined that pact in 1882, forming the Triple Alliance. For 10 points, name this German “Iron Chancellor” who united Germany in 1871.

tossups.p: After two attempts on the life of Kaiser Wilhelm I, this man pushed through Anti-Socialist Laws that banned socialist meetings and newspapers. To win workers away from socialism, he also created the world’s first national health insurance program in 1883.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this “Iron Chancellor” who built an early welfare state in Germany.

tossups.p: This man hosted the Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885, where European powers set rules for claiming land in Africa. Germany gained colonies such as Togoland and Cameroon while he was chancellor, even though he had long doubted that colonies were worth the cost.
tossups.r: The capital of North Dakota is named for him. For 10 points, name this first chancellor of the German Empire.

tossups.p: After Prussia defeated Austria in 1866, this statesman joined the German states north of the Main River into the North German Confederation. Four years later, he set off a war with France that ended with Germany taking Alsace-Lorraine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Prussian leader who became the German Empire’s first chancellor, famous for his “blood and iron” speech.

tossups.p: This man shortened a telegram describing King Wilhelm I’s meeting with the French ambassador, Count Benedetti [“beh-neh-DET-ee”], so that the meeting sounded insulting to both sides. After he released that Ems Dispatch to the press, France declared war in July 1870.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Prussian “Iron Chancellor” who then won the Franco-Prussian War and united Germany.

tossups.p: A famous painting by Anton von Werner shows this man at the center of the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles as Wilhelm I is proclaimed German Emperor in January 1871. Months earlier, Prussian-led armies had captured Napoleon III at the Battle of Sedan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this statesman who became the first chancellor of the united Germany.

tossups.p: This chancellor’s fiercest opponent in parliament was Ludwig Windthorst [“VINT-horst”], leader of the Catholic Centre Party, which grew stronger during this chancellor’s campaign against the Church. This chancellor eased that campaign after Pope Leo XIII took office in 1878.
tossups.r: That campaign was called the Kulturkampf. For 10 points, name this “Iron Chancellor” of Germany.

tossups.p: Before leading Prussia, this practitioner of Realpolitik [“ray-AHL-poh-lee-teek”] served as ambassador to Russia in St. Petersburg and then to France. As Prussia’s leader, he allied with Austria to defeat Denmark in 1864 and take the duchies of Schleswig [“SHLAYS-vig”] and Holstein.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this statesman who then defeated Austria and France on the way to uniting Germany.

tossups.p: This leader’s government passed an Accident Insurance Law in 1884 and an Old Age and Disability Insurance Law in 1889, giving German workers some of the world’s first public pensions. He hoped those programs would weaken support for the Social Democrats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this “Iron Chancellor” who unified Germany after the Franco-Prussian War.

tossups.p: Born in 1815 into a family of Prussian Junkers [“YOONG-kers”], or landowning nobles, this man told a budget committee in 1862 that the great mistake of 1848 and 1849 had been trying to settle big questions through speeches and majority votes.
tossups.r: He said they would be settled instead by “iron and blood.” For 10 points, name this Prussian statesman who later unified Germany.

trap.body: Bismarck served Germany’s emperors but was never one himself. topics.name: Battle of Waterloo
topics.kicker: Napoleon’s final defeat, 1815 · Ended his comeback and his rule
topics.briefing: On June 18, 1815, near the village of Waterloo in what is now Belgium, Napoleon gambled everything on one last battle against the Duke of Wellington’s army. Wellington’s troops held their ridge all afternoon against French attacks, and by evening Gebhard von Blücher’s Prussians had arrived to help finish the job. Napoleon gave up his throne four days later and was exiled to Saint Helena, and “meeting your Waterloo” still means facing a final defeat.

tossups.p: A huge artificial hill topped by a statue of a lion marks roughly where the Prince of Orange, the future King William II of the Netherlands, was wounded in this battle. Fighting in this battle also raged all day around the walled farm of Hougoumont [“OO-goo-mohn”].

tossups.p: A deadly 1819 cavalry charge into a crowd demanding voting reform at St. Peter’s Field in Manchester was nicknamed the Peterloo Massacre, a bitter joke on this battle’s name. This battle came two days after Napoleon beat the Prussians at Ligny [“leen-YEE”].
tossups.r: The Duke of Wellington won it. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle in Belgium, Napoleon’s final defeat.

tossups.p: Napoleon sent Marshal Emmanuel de Grouchy [“groo-SHEE”] with a large part of his army to chase the Prussians, but Grouchy fought at Wavre [“WAHV-ruh”] and missed this battle. Meanwhile, the Prussians hit the French right flank at the village of Plancenoit [“plahns-NWAH”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1815 battle, where Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher defeated Napoleon.

tossups.p: Many British officers left the Duchess of Richmond’s ball in Brussels to join the campaign that ended in this battle, some still wearing their evening clothes. Two days before this battle, Wellington’s army fought the French at the crossroads of Quatre Bras [“KAH-truh BRAH”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of June 18, 1815, which ended Napoleon’s Hundred Days.

tossups.p: Heavy rain the night before this battle turned the fields to mud, so Napoleon waited until late morning to attack, giving the Prussians more time to arrive. The first French attack in this battle struck the walled château and farm of Hougoumont [“OO-goo-mohn”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1815 battle in which Napoleon lost to the Duke of Wellington.

tossups.p: Soldiers of the King’s German Legion held the farmhouse of La Haye Sainte [“lah AY SANT”] at the center of this battle until their ammunition ran out. That same afternoon, British infantry squares fought off huge French cavalry charges led by Marshal Ney.
tossups.r: Blücher’s Prussians helped win it. For 10 points, name this battle where Napoleon was finally defeated in 1815.

tossups.p: The winning commander in this battle sheltered many of his troops behind the crest of a low ridge so that French cannonballs would fly over them. Afterward, he called this battle “the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life.”
tossups.r: That commander was the Duke of Wellington. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle, Napoleon’s final defeat.

tossups.p: In the evening of this battle, Napoleon sent his elite Imperial Guard up the slope in a last attack, and the French army fell apart after the Guard was driven back. Napoleon gave up his throne four days later.
tossups.r: The Duke of Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher commanded the winning armies. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle.

tossups.p: In _Les Misérables_, Victor Hugo spends many chapters on this battle, in which the crook Thénardier [“tay-nar-DYAY”] robs a wounded French officer who thinks Thénardier has saved his life. That officer, Colonel Pontmercy, is the father of the student Marius.
tossups.r: Today, this battle’s name means any final, crushing defeat. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle in Belgium.

tossups.p: Diplomats at the Congress of Vienna were still redrawing the map of Europe when Napoleon escaped from Elba, and they signed their Final Act just nine days before this battle. In this battle, the armies of the Seventh Coalition defeated Napoleon for good.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle in modern Belgium that ended Napoleon’s Hundred Days.

tossups.p: Two days before this battle, the 72-year-old Prussian commander Gebhard von Blücher [“BLOO-kur”] was trapped under his fallen horse at Ligny [“leen-YEE”]. He recovered in time to march his army toward this battle anyway.
tossups.r: His Prussians arrived in the afternoon to help the Duke of Wellington win. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle, Napoleon’s last.

tossups.p: About a month after this battle, its loser surrendered to Captain Frederick Maitland aboard the British warship HMS _Bellerophon_. The British then sent him to the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he died six years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this battle of June 18, 1815, Napoleon’s final defeat.

tossups.p: In William Makepeace Thackeray’s novel _Vanity Fair_, Amelia Sedley waits anxiously in Brussels while her husband, George Osborne, marches off and is killed in this battle. After this battle, King Louis XVIII returned to Paris and took back the French throne.
tossups.r: Wellington and Blücher won it. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle, the final defeat of Napoleon.

tossups.p: Napoleon hoped to defeat the British and Prussian armies one at a time before they could join forces, so he invaded what was then the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. His plan failed in this battle, fought near a village south of Brussels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1815 battle in which the Duke of Wellington and Blücher ended Napoleon’s Hundred Days.

tossups.p: The winning general in this battle rode his chestnut horse Copenhagen for many hours during the fighting. That general had earlier beaten the French in Spain and Portugal during the Peninsular War.
tossups.r: That general was the Duke of Wellington. For 10 points, name this 1815 battle in Belgium where Napoleon met his final defeat.

trap.title: Battle or emperor?
trap.body: Waterloo tossups are packed with Napoleon clues (the Hundred Days, Elba, Saint Helena), so it is easy to blurt out “Napoleon” when the question wants the battle, or to say “Waterloo” on a Napoleon question that ends “name this emperor.” Players also mix up the battles of that week: Ligny and Quatre Bras were fought on June 16, two days before this one. And one real Napoleonic Wars tossup only prompts on Waterloo, because it wants the whole war.
trap.fix: Listen to the last line: “name this battle” wants Waterloo, “name this emperor” wants Napoleon, and “name this conflict” wants the Napoleonic Wars. Waterloo is the one where Wellington and Blücher won together, with fighting at Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte and Marshal Ney’s cavalry charges.

topics.name: Magna Carta
topics.kicker: King John’s 1215 charter limiting royal power · Sealed at Runnymede
topics.briefing: In June 1215, England’s rebellious barons forced King John to seal a charter at Runnymede, a meadow by the Thames, after his allies lost a key battle in France and he badly mismanaged the kingdom’s finances. Magna Carta — Latin for “Great Charter” — limited royal power, protected the barons’ rights, and even banned certain fish traps on rivers. Though Pope Innocent III quickly tried to cancel it, its due-process ideas later shaped English law and inspired the U.S. Constitution.

tossups.p: The 18th-century jurist William Blackstone later numbered this document’s clauses from 1 to 63. One original copy of this document is thought to have gone to a group of English ports known as the Cinque [“sink”] Ports, while others went to cathedrals around the kingdom.
tossups.r: Drafted largely by Stephen Langton, the Archbishop of Canterbury, this document was meant to settle a dispute between a king and his barons. For 10 points, name this 1215 charter sealed at Runnymede by King John of England.

tossups.p: King John had made England a fief of the Pope back in 1213, a move that later let him appeal for this document’s annulment. John agreed to this document only after Philip II of France crushed his allies at the Battle of Bouvines [“boo-VEEN”], forcing John to sue for peace.
tossups.r: Pope Innocent III soon declared this document invalid anyway. For 10 points, name this 1215 English charter, sealed at Runnymede by King John.

tossups.p: This document’s sixty-first clause let a council of twenty-five barons seize the king’s lands and castles if he broke its terms. When King John ignored that threat, rebel barons led by Robert Fitzwalter rose up in the First Barons’ War and invited the future French king Louis VIII to invade England.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter that English barons forced King John to seal at Runnymede.

tossups.p: A companion document called the Charter of the Forest eased harsh royal forest laws soon after this charter first appeared, ending the death penalty for poaching deer. This earlier document itself banned certain fish-weir traps from blocking England’s rivers.

tossups.p: This document’s thirty-ninth clause said a free man could be punished only by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, an early statement of due process. Historians often credit it with introducing ideas related to habeas corpus into English law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter whose due-process ideas later influenced the U.S. Constitution.

tossups.p: This document’s very first clause guaranteed the freedom of the English Church, while its thirteenth clause confirmed the City of London’s ancient liberties. Most of its sixty-three clauses, though, dealt with narrower feudal privileges that no longer apply today.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter sealed by King John at Runnymede under pressure from his barons.

tossups.p: After the king who first sealed this document died in 1216, his nine-year-old son Henry III quickly reissued it to win back rebel barons’ support. The version with lasting legal authority actually comes from a further reissue of this document in 1225.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this charter, originally sealed in 1215 by King John at Runnymede.

tossups.p: This document’s guarantees technically applied only to “free men,” a minority in a society where most people were unfree peasants bound to the land. Despite that narrow original scope, its rule-of-law ideas eventually helped inspire constitutions worldwide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter, sealed at Runnymede, whose Latin name translates to roughly “big charter.”

tossups.p: Pope Innocent III declared this document null and void within weeks of its sealing, siding with the king against his barons. That annulment helped trigger England’s First Barons’ War soon afterward.
tossups.r: Despite the Pope’s objection, this document survived in reissued form for centuries. For 10 points, name this 1215 charter forced on King John by rebellious barons.

tossups.p: Stephen Langton, the Archbishop of Canterbury, helped draft this document in an attempt to prevent open war between King John and his barons. It failed in the short term, since John’s refusal to honor it helped start the First Barons’ War anyway.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter sealed in a meadow called Runnymede.

tossups.p: Rebel barons who felt King John had broken this document invited Louis, the future King Louis VIII of France, to invade England and claim the throne. Those same barons had rebelled partly because John’s allies had been crushed at the Battle of Bouvines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter, which John had sealed at Runnymede under baronial pressure.

tossups.p: Copies of this document were distributed to cathedrals and, it is thought, to the Cinque Ports after it was sealed. Centuries later, William Blackstone organized its text into the numbered clauses still used today, including one guaranteeing the freedom of the English Church.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter that King John sealed at Runnymede.

tossups.p: Among its more specific provisions, this document ordered the removal of fish-weir traps from England’s rivers and promised that free men would face only lawful judgment by their peers. A companion charter dealing with royal forests followed a few years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter that barons forced King John to seal at Runnymede, limiting royal power.

tossups.p: Clauses of this document promising “lawful judgment” and protection from arbitrary imprisonment later echoed through English common law and across the Atlantic. Drafted by Stephen Langton to end a crisis between a king and his barons, it originally protected only “free men.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter whose ideas influenced the U.S. Constitution and Bill of Rights.

tossups.p: After his allies lost the Battle of Bouvines, King John sealed this document at Runnymede, only to see Pope Innocent III annul it within weeks. His son Henry III later reissued it to help end the war that followed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1215 charter whose Latin name refers to its great size and importance.

trap.title: Which charter, which crisis?
trap.body: Medieval England produced a whole family of “charter” and “rights” documents, and it’s easy to mix them up: Henry I’s 1100 Charter of Liberties came a century earlier, the Charter of the Forest is a separate companion document about forest law, the Provisions of Oxford (1258) and the English Bill of Rights (1689) are later constitutional moments, and King John himself is a person, not a document.

tossups.p: After capturing its new capital, this empire converted the great church of Hagia Sophia into a mosque. In 1826, Sultan Mahmud II abolished this empire’s once-feared Janissary corps, a group originally built from Christian boys taken under the devshirme system.
tossups.r: This empire later tried to modernize through the 1800s Tanzimat reforms. For 10 points, name this empire ruled from Istanbul and nicknamed the “Sick Man of Europe.”

tossups.p: The 1920 Treaty of Sèvres proposed dividing up this empire’s remaining territory among the Allied powers, but Turkish nationalists rejected it and fought back. Mehmed VI, this empire’s last sultan, left the country in 1922 as its sultanate was formally abolished.
tossups.r: The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne then recognized the new Republic of Turkey in its place. For 10 points, name this empire once ruled by Suleiman the Magnificent, which collapsed after World War I.

tossups.p: This empire’s troops defeated a British-led force at the Siege of Kut during World War I, after earlier turning back an Allied landing at Gallipoli, where a young officer named Mustafa Kemal made his name.
tossups.r: This empire had joined the war on the side of the Central Powers, alongside Germany and Austria-Hungary. For 10 points, name this empire of sultans, ruled from Istanbul and nicknamed the “Sick Man of Europe.”

tossups.p: Sultan Selim the Grim expanded this empire’s rule into Egypt and the Middle East, and after his forces conquered the Mamluk Sultanate in 1517, this empire’s rulers began also calling themselves caliphs. Young Christian boys were recruited into this empire’s service under the devshirme system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Islamic empire led at its peak by Suleiman the Magnificent, which lasted until just after World War I.

tossups.p: A chieftain named Osman I founded this state around 1299 in Anatolia, and by 1526 its armies were crushing Hungary at the Battle of Mohács. A Catholic alliance finally stopped this empire’s expansion into central Europe at the 1683 Siege of Vienna.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this empire that collapsed after World War I, leading to the creation of the modern nation of Turkey.

tossups.p: Admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa helped this empire dominate much of the Mediterranean Sea in the first half of the 1500s, though a Holy League fleet later defeated this empire’s navy at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571. In the 1800s, this empire’s Tanzimat reforms tried to modernize its government.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this empire ruled from Istanbul by sultans such as Suleiman the Magnificent, nicknamed the “Sick Man of Europe” in its final century.

trap.title: Empire, not Turkey
trap.body: Several real packets specifically rule that “Turkey” does not earn credit for this empire, since modern Turkey is the separate nation Mustafa Kemal Ataturk founded after this empire dissolved. Players also mix this empire up with the Byzantine Empire it conquered in 1453, and with the rival Safavid Empire next door in Persia.
trap.fix: If the clues describe sultans, Istanbul, or events before 1922, give the empire’s name, not “Turkey” — and give the state’s name, not a ruler’s name like Suleiman, since the question wants the empire, not the person.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ottoman Empire (do not accept or prompt on “Turkey”)
